headline.headline: GOLDEN KNIGHTS STRIPPED OF DRAFT PICK, COACH TORTORELLA HIT WITH $100K FINE
headline.deck: NHL hands Vegas stiff punishment after team boxes out media during second round
headline.body:
The NHL dropped the hammer on the Vegas Golden Knights on Friday, stripping the franchise of a second-round draft pick and fining head coach John Tortorella $100,000 after the team deliberately blocked media access during the second round of the playoffs. The league's ruling, announced Friday, represents one of the stiffest penalties levied against a franchise in recent postseason memory and sends a clear message to all 32 clubs that obstructing press operations will not be tolerated at any stage of the playoffs.

Tortorella, the 67-year-old coach known for his combustible personality and frequent run-ins with reporters over a career spanning three decades behind an NHL bench, was personally implicated in the incident. The Golden Knights organization did not immediately contest the ruling, though team officials were expected to address the matter Saturday. The loss of a second-round pick carries significant long-term consequences for a Vegas roster that has relied on savvy drafting and trades to remain a perennial contender.

The timing could not be worse for a Golden Knights club already navigating the pressure of a deep playoff run. Vegas now faces the distraction of league discipline hanging over the franchise as it prepares for conference finals positioning, with the Colorado Avalanche looming as a potential opponent in the Western Conference Finals. For Tortorella, the fine adds another chapter to one of the most turbulent coaching careers in NHL history.

secondary.headline: SNELL LANDS ON IL WITH ELBOW TROUBLE, RAISING FRESH FEARS FOR DODGERS
secondary.deck: Two-time Cy Young winner sidelined with loose bodies in his elbow less than a week after his last start
secondary.body:
Blake Snell, the two-time Cy Young Award winner signed by the Los Angeles Dodgers to anchor a rotation already brimming with talent, has been placed on the injured list with loose bodies in his elbow, the club announced Friday. The move comes fewer than seven days after his most recent outing, and while the Dodgers offered cautious optimism that surgery would not be required, the situation drew immediate concern across a franchise that has watched pitching injuries derail championship windows before.

Snell, 33, struggled to find consistency through the early weeks of the 2026 season, posting middling numbers that already had Dodgers fans anxious. The elbow diagnosis deepens those concerns considerably. Los Angeles has the rotation depth to absorb short-term absence, but a prolonged IL stint for Snell would test even the Dodgers' considerable pitching resources as the National League pennant race intensifies through the summer months.

secondary.headline: HARDEN PASSES CURRY ON ALL-TIME POSTSEASON SCORING LIST WITH STEP-BACK THREE
secondary.deck: James Harden's vintage pull-up three-pointer moves him into 10th place in NBA playoff history
secondary.body:
James Harden needed just one shot to etch his name deeper into NBA history Friday night. The veteran guard drilled a step-back three-pointer to surpass Stephen Curry and claim 10th place on the NBA's all-time postseason scoring list, a milestone that arrived with the flair Harden has delivered throughout a playoff career defined by isolation brilliance and late-game shot-making. The basket brought a roar from the crowd and a moment of reflection for a player who has spent years accumulating postseason points despite persistent criticism of his championship credentials.

Harden's ascent up the all-time list comes during a conference semifinals run that has reminded observers why he remains one of the most difficult offensive players to guard in basketball. Curry, who was passed on the list by a player who has long been compared and contrasted with the Warriors legend, finished his career with 3,695 postseason points. Harden moved past that mark Friday and shows no signs of slowing down as the second round reaches its decisive games.

secondary.headline: FORMER NFL LINEMAN JOSH MAURO DIED FROM FENTANYL, COCAINE AND ALCOHOL COMBINATION
secondary.deck: Medical examiner rules Mauro's death an acute drug and alcohol intoxication; NFL mourns the loss
secondary.body:
Former NFL defensive lineman Josh Mauro died from an acute combination of fentanyl, cocaine and ethanol intoxication, according to the findings of a medical examiner released Friday. Mauro, who played for several franchises over a professional career that included stints with the New England Patriots and Las Vegas Raiders, was found dead earlier this year. The ruling closes the official inquiry into the cause of death and adds his name to a heartbreaking list of former players lost to substance-related causes.

The NFL Players Association and several former teammates acknowledged Mauro's passing with statements Friday, with many calling for continued expansion of mental health and substance abuse resources for both active players and alumni. Mauro was 33. His death drew renewed attention to the league's post-career support programs and reignited a conversation about the physical and psychological toll that professional football imposes on players long after their final snap.

column.headline: TORTORELLA CROSSED A LINE, AND THE NHL WAS RIGHT TO MAKE HIM PAY FOR IT
column.body:
John Tortorella has spent a lifetime testing boundaries. He has berated reporters, stormed off podiums and treated press conferences like inconvenient interruptions to the real business of hockey. Fans have often cheered him for it, celebrating the gruff act as authenticity in a league that sometimes drowns in corporate-speak. But physically boxing out media members is not authenticity. It is obstruction, and the NHL was absolutely correct to strip Vegas of a draft pick and fine Tortorella $100,000 for it. The penalty had to sting. A slap on the wrist would have meant nothing to a coach who has never mistaken a fine for a deterrent.

The draft pick is the part that matters most. Fines are easily absorbed by franchises worth billions of dollars. Taking away a second-round pick forces the Golden Knights organization to feel the consequences in the place it hurts most: the future of the roster. If the league wants to protect press access during the playoffs, when public accountability is at its highest, it cannot rely on token gestures. Friday's ruling was not perfect, but it was a start. And Tortorella, for all his undeniable coaching gifts, should know better at 67 than to let a team he leads bully the people whose job it is to cover the game.

story.headline: REDS PUMMEL NATIONALS 15-1 IN HISTORIC ROUT
story.deck: Cincinnati erupts for 15 runs, hands Washington its most lopsided loss of the season
story.body:
WASHINGTON — The Cincinnati Reds turned Nationals Park into a house of horrors Thursday, pounding the Washington Nationals 15-1 in a rout so thorough it left the home crowd filing toward the exits before the seventh-inning stretch. The Reds sent 11 batters to the plate in a single inning and racked up hits in bunches, turning what looked like a competitive ballgame into a mercy-rule candidate from the middle frames onward.

The carnage was spread across the Cincinnati lineup, with multiple Reds reaching base repeatedly against a Washington pitching staff that could not find an answer. The Nationals, who have struggled to piece together consistent starting pitching all spring, watched their bullpen absorb the bulk of the punishment as manager Dave Martinez burned through relievers trying to stanch the bleeding. Washington managed just one run against a Cincinnati rotation that has quietly become one of the more reliable in the National League.

The lopsided victory pushed Cincinnati further above .500 and cemented a troubling trend for the Nationals, who have now surrendered double-digit runs three times this month. Pittsburgh's 7-2 win over Colorado, Minnesota's 9-1 thrashing of Miami and Milwaukee's 7-1 victory over San Diego rounded out a Thursday slate dominated by offense, but nothing matched the sheer spectacle of the Reds' demolition job in the nation's capital.

story.headline: WILLIAMS DECLARES HIMSELF READY AS THUNDER PREPARE FOR WESTERN CONFERENCE FINALS
story.deck: Oklahoma City's star wing returns from hamstring injury at the perfect moment.
story.body:
OKLAHOMA CITY — Jalen Williams walked into practice Thursday without a limp, without a wrap and without hesitation, declaring himself fully healthy after a six-game absence caused by a Grade 1 left hamstring strain. The Thunder wing, considered Oklahoma City's most versatile offensive weapon heading into the Western Conference Finals, said the extra rest turned out to be a blessing. Williams averaged 23.4 points, 5.1 rebounds and 4.8 assists in the first two rounds before the injury forced him to the bench, and the Thunder survived without him — a testament to the depth coach Mark Daigneault has built around this roster.

The timing could not be better for a Thunder team that will need every healthy body available against a Western Conference Finals opponent still to be determined. Williams spent his recovery sessions working with the training staff on hamstring strengthening and watching extensive film, and he insisted Friday that he feels sharper mentally for the time spent away from game action. Oklahoma City went 4-2 in his absence, leaning heavily on Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and a swarming defensive rotation that ranked first in the postseason in opponent field-goal percentage.

Elsewhere around the league Friday, OG Anunoby returned to full practice with the Knicks ahead of their upcoming Eastern Conference Finals home opener, delivering a significant boost to a New York squad that had been managing his workload carefully for two weeks. Meanwhile, James Harden etched his name deeper into playoff history, passing Stephen Curry for 10th place on the all-time postseason scoring list with a vintage step-back three-pointer, a fitting shot for a player who has built his entire career around that singular, maddening move.

story.headline: RANGERS ROUT CAPS, HURRICANES SMOTHER PANTHERS TO ADVANCE IN EAST
story.deck: New York and Carolina punch tickets with dominant playoff victories Thursday night.
story.body:
The New York Rangers turned Madison Square Garden into a thunderdome Thursday night, rolling past the Washington Capitals 6-3 in a performance that was never as close as the final score suggested. Artemi Panarin was everywhere, orchestrating the offense with a relentless forecheck that had Washington's blue line retreating all evening. Igor Shesterkin was sharp when called upon, and the Garden crowd was in full roar from the drop of the first puck.

In the nightcap, the Carolina Hurricanes suffocated the Florida Panthers 5-1 in a masterclass of defensive structure and opportunistic offense. Sebastian Aho buried two goals as Carolina's vaunted forechecking system turned the Panthers' transition game into rubble. Florida, the reigning Eastern Conference power, looked a step slow throughout, and goaltender Sergei Bobrovsky was pulled after surrendering his fourth goal midway through the third period.

The results set up a marquee Eastern Conference Final matchup that the league could not have scripted better. The Rangers bring their star power and the Garden mystique, while the Hurricanes arrive battle-hardened and playing perhaps their most complete hockey of the Rod Brind'Amour era. Game 1 is scheduled for Sunday night.

story.headline: RAMS ROLL THE DICE ON VETERAN QUARTERBACK AS OFFSEASON RESHUFFLES NFC WEST
story.deck: Los Angeles makes a bold move while draft picks settle into new homes across the league.
story.body:
The Los Angeles Rams wasted no time reshaping their roster this spring, agreeing to terms with veteran quarterback Russell Wilson on a two-year deal worth up to $52 million, sources confirmed Tuesday. The move signals a dramatic philosophical shift for a franchise that spent the better part of a decade building around Matthew Stafford, who was released in March following a shoulder injury that cost him the final six weeks of the 2025 season. Wilson, 37, threw for 22 touchdowns with the Pittsburgh Steelers last fall before becoming a free agent in February, and head coach Sean McVay believes the mobile signal-caller still has enough left in the tank to compete for an NFC West title.

The 2026 NFL Draft, held last month in Indianapolis, continued to reshape rosters across the league, with the Tennessee Titans selecting defensive end Marcus Holloway out of Georgia with the second overall pick. Holloway, a consensus All-American who registered 14 sacks in his final college season, has already reported to Nashville for voluntary workouts and drawn rave reviews from the coaching staff. Meanwhile, the New England Patriots used three of their first four selections on offensive linemen, a clear signal that first-year head coach Mike Vrabel intends to rebuild the franchise from the trenches outward after consecutive losing seasons.

Around the rest of the league, the Dallas Cowboys parted ways with wide receiver CeeDee Lamb in a stunning trade that sent the four-time Pro Bowler to the Miami Dolphins in exchange for two first-round picks and cornerback Jalen Ramsey. Cowboys owner Jerry Jones defended the move at a press conference Monday, calling it a necessary step toward long-term financial flexibility. Lamb, who turns 27 in June, is expected to give Dolphins quarterback Tua Tagovailoa a legitimate No. 1 target for the first time in years, and Miami's front office described the deal as the centerpiece of a broader push to return to the playoffs after missing the postseason in 2025.
